section_summary: This section chiefly documents a wave of letters and petitions from clergy, missionaries, church members, and peace activists urging the Roosevelt administration to halt American exports of arms, aircraft, scrap iron, oil, and other materials to Japan during the Sino-Japanese War. State Department replies repeatedly explain that, without a presidential proclamation recognizing a state of war, the Neutrality Act does not permit an arms embargo and in any event does not cover raw materials such as scrap iron. The section also contains internal memoranda, export-license figures, press summaries, information on international loans and investments, and an editorial arguing that American supplies enabled Japan's bombing of Chinese civilians.

subfiles.title: Letter to Lloyd S. Ruland concerning an embargo on war materials to Japan
subfiles.from: Charles W. Yost, Acting Chief, Office of Arms and Munitions Control
subfiles.to: Lloyd S. Ruland, China Secretary, Board of Foreign Missions of the Presbyterian Church in the U.S.A.
subfiles.about: Responds to Ruland's request, based on a missionary's cable, for an embargo on war materials exported to Japan.
subfiles.summary: Yost explains that the Neutrality Act would prohibit arms exports to both China and Japan only if the President proclaimed that a state of war existed. He says the President judged invocation contrary to American interests, supplies export-license totals for both countries, and recalls the Secretary of State's condemnation of bombing civilian populations and its material encouragement.

subfiles.title: Colcord Avenue Methodist Church petition to curtail supplies to Japan
subfiles.from: H. M. Hopkins and other citizens associated with Colcord Avenue Methodist Church
subfiles.about: Petitions the Secretary of State to curtail shipments of oil, scrap iron, and other raw materials that could prolong Japan's war in China.
subfiles.summary: The petition argues that Japan depends upon American oil, scrap iron, and other commodities to continue the war. Numerous Waco-area church members sign the appeal, although several handwritten names are poorly captured by the OCR.

subfiles.title: Reply to H. M. Hopkins and the Colcord Avenue petitioners
subfiles.from: Charles W. Yost, Acting Chief, Office of Arms and Munitions Control
subfiles.about: Explains the statutory limits on restricting arms and raw-material exports to Japan.
subfiles.summary: Yost states that an arms embargo under the Joint Resolution would require a presidential proclamation of war and would then apply equally to China and Japan. He adds that the law gives no power to prohibit other commodities, says invocation would not serve American interests, and reports licensed arms exports to both belligerents.

subfiles.title: Charge slip for file 894.24
subfiles.from: Department of State filing staff
subfiles.about: Records internal charges or withdrawals of material from file 894.24.
subfiles.summary: The form lists several offices, initials, numbers, and dates associated with the file or an enclosure. Its terse administrative entries do not identify the subject matter of the charged item.

subfiles.title: Memorandum requesting a paragraph on loans to Japan
subfiles.from: Division of Far Eastern Affairs
subfiles.to: Office of Arms and Munitions Control
subfiles.about: Suggests language from an appended mimeographed letter for answering a request about loans to Japan.
subfiles.summary: The memorandum says that a member of the recipient division left an attached letter and requested a paragraph on loans to Japan. It recommends using the second paragraph of the appended mimeographed letter.

subfiles.title: Letter from George D. and Gertrude S. Wilder on war supplies, credits, and aid to China
subfiles.from: George D. Wilder and Gertrude S. Wilder
subfiles.about: Urges an end to sales and credits supporting Japan and requests material aid for China.
subfiles.summary: The Wilders, preparing to return to Peiping, fear that Americans will be blamed for supplying much of Japan's war material and ask whether the Department can prevent suppliers from extending credit. They also mention Byron N. Scott's congressional resolution and argue that official action should reflect widespread American sympathy for China.

subfiles.title: Mimeographed letter to Alvin L. Schorr on loans, credits, and investments
subfiles.from: Maxwell M. Hamilton, Chief, Division of Far Eastern Affairs
subfiles.about: Provides information on loans, commercial credits, and American and British investments in China and Japan.
subfiles.summary: Hamilton says the Department knows of no American loans to Japanese or Chinese borrowers since July 1937, apart from ordinary commercial credits about which it lacks detailed information. He supplies published figures for American investments, describes other American financial and institutional interests in China, and refers Schorr to G. F. Remer's estimate of British investments.

subfiles.title: Reply to George D. Wilder
subfiles.from: Charles W. Yost, Acting Chief, Office of Arms and Munitions Control
subfiles.about: Answers Wilder's questions about war-material exports and possible Japanese credits in the United States.
subfiles.summary: Yost repeats that the Neutrality Act could be invoked only through a presidential war proclamation and that it does not authorize restrictions on commodities outside the statutory arms list. He reports export-license values and says the Department has no information about Japanese borrowing beyond normal commercial credits.

subfiles.title: Cross-reference note for Hankow Despatch No. 453
subfiles.from: Department of State filing staff
subfiles.about: Directs the reader to a Hankow despatch concerning Chinese appreciation of efforts to discourage aircraft sales to Japan.
subfiles.summary: The file note cross-references Despatch No. 453 from Hankow, associated with Josselyn. It summarizes the subject as the sale of American war supplies to Japan and favorable reaction to discouraging American aircraft sales.

subfiles.title: Chinese press reaction to discouraging American airplane sales to Japan
subfiles.about: Summarizes favorable Chinese newspaper reaction to American steps discouraging aircraft sales to Japan.
subfiles.summary: The item says the American announcement made a highly favorable impression in Chinese circles. It quotes or paraphrases Chinese newspapers welcoming the blow to Japan, asking for an explicit legal prohibition, and urging American exporters to comply voluntarily.

subfiles.title: Egbert W. Smith's appeal to President Roosevelt
subfiles.from: Egbert W. Smith
subfiles.about: Asks the President to end American participation in supplying Japan with materials used against China.
subfiles.summary: Smith cites the Foreign Policy Bulletin's claim that only Western refusal to supply Japan can end China's devastation. He describes mounting American indignation and calls it inconsistent to furnish Japan with resources while soliciting relief for Chinese victims.

subfiles.title: Acknowledgment to Egbert W. Smith
subfiles.from: Charles W. Yost, Acting Chief, Office of Arms and Munitions Control
subfiles.about: Acknowledges Smith's letter after its referral from the White House.
subfiles.summary: Yost acknowledges Smith's July 20 letter concerning the Far Eastern situation. He directs Smith to Hull's August 2 reply to another letter from Smith on the same subject.

subfiles.title: James V. Claypool's letter opposing shipments to Japan
subfiles.from: James V. Claypool
subfiles.about: Urges Roosevelt and Hull to prevent further shipments of munitions and other war-making resources to Japan.
subfiles.summary: Claypool describes scrap iron being loaded at nearby docks and argues that denying Japan material assistance might reduce the need for American naval expansion. Identifying himself as a veteran, Legion member, and reserve Navy chaplain, he asks that the Neutrality Act be applied.

subfiles.title: Reply to James V. Claypool
subfiles.from: Charles W. Yost, Acting Chief, Office of Arms and Munitions Control
subfiles.about: Explains why the administration had not invoked the Neutrality Act or prohibited raw-material exports.
subfiles.summary: The reply states that a presidential proclamation would prohibit arms exports to both China and Japan, while no such proclamation had been issued. It explains that other commodities fall outside the statute, defends the President's discretion, and gives current licensed arms-export totals.

subfiles.title: National Holiness Missionary Society protest against war-equipment sales
subfiles.from: Salome C. Troe and Mrs. J. B. Hill for the National Holiness Missionary Society, California State Auxiliary
subfiles.about: Reports the organization's unanimous protest against selling instruments of war to Japan.
subfiles.summary: The California auxiliary condemns Japanese aggression against China and asserts that American war implements facilitate it. The organization asks Hull to use his office to prevent further sales of war equipment to Japan.

subfiles.title: Reply to Mrs. J. B. Hill
subfiles.from: Charles W. Yost, Acting Chief, Office of Arms and Munitions Control
subfiles.about: Responds to the National Holiness Missionary Society's protest against exports to Japan.
subfiles.summary: Yost explains that the Joint Resolution would prohibit arms exports to both belligerents only following a presidential proclamation. He says the President considered invocation contrary to the national interest and provides licensed-export figures for China and Japan.

subfiles.title: Sam Hedrick's appeal to end war-sustaining traffic with Japan
subfiles.from: Sam Hedrick
subfiles.about: Urges the President to end trade that makes the United States a partner in Japan's war against China.
subfiles.summary: Hedrick characterizes American-Japanese trade in war-supporting goods as participation in the Far Eastern conflict. He stresses the destruction of Chinese lives and property and invokes the historically friendly relationship between Americans and Chinese.

subfiles.title: Reply to Sam Hedrick
subfiles.from: For the Secretary of State; individual signatory not visible in the OCR
subfiles.about: Explains the administration's position on invoking the Neutrality Act against exports to China and Japan.
subfiles.summary: The reply says an embargo would require a presidential proclamation and would apply to arms shipments to both countries. It defends the President's refusal to invoke the law and provides recent export-license totals.

subfiles.title: C. Hafer Morgan's letter transmitting a church petition
subfiles.from: C. Hafer Morgan
subfiles.about: Transmits a petition signed by members of St. John's Church opposing American aid to the invaders of China.
subfiles.summary: Morgan says the petition originated at the Kanuga Conferences and attracted strong interest among the Columbia congregation. He expresses concern that the United States is aiding China's invaders for profit and hopes the petition will help restrain that trade.

subfiles.title: St. John's Church petition against exports used for war
subfiles.from: Members of St. John's Church, Columbia, South Carolina
subfiles.about: Petitions the President to stop shipments of scrap iron, steel, oil, cotton, and other war materials to countries bombing civilians.
subfiles.summary: The petition praises the government's appeal to airplane manufacturers but argues that continuing exports of other strategic commodities is self-contradictory. Church members ask the President to end shipments that facilitate international lawlessness and killing.

subfiles.title: Reply to C. Hafer Morgan
subfiles.from: Charles W. Yost, Acting Chief, Office of Arms and Munitions Control
subfiles.about: Acknowledges the St. John's Church petition and explains the legal limits on an embargo.
subfiles.summary: Yost welcomes the petition's approval of Hull's statement discouraging aircraft sales to countries bombing civilians. He explains that the Neutrality Act would affect both China and Japan after a war proclamation, cannot reach most raw materials, and had not been invoked because of broader American interests.

subfiles.title: John Henry Hopkins's handwritten appeal against munitions exports
subfiles.from: John Henry Hopkins
subfiles.about: Pleads for action to stop the sale of American munitions to Japan.
subfiles.summary: Hopkins describes the war against China as infamous and imposed by barbarous forces controlling Japan. He asks the Secretary to do everything possible to end American assistance to it.

subfiles.title: Reply to John Henry Hopkins
subfiles.from: Charles W. Yost, Acting Chief, Office of Arms and Munitions Control
subfiles.about: Answers Hopkins's request for an embargo on munitions to Japan.
subfiles.summary: Yost says the Neutrality Act would halt arms exports to both sides only after a presidential finding that a state of war existed. He explains the President's refusal to invoke the statute and cites export-license values for China and Japan.

subfiles.title: Memorandum on public demands for an embargo
subfiles.from: R. V. Haig, Office of Arms and Munitions Control
subfiles.about: Reports monthly totals of letters, telegrams, and postcards favoring an embargo on shipments to Japan.
subfiles.summary: Haig reports that the office received 308 letters and telegrams and 2,795 postcards supporting an embargo during July. For comparison, June brought 644 letters and telegrams and 725 postcards on the same issue.

subfiles.title: Roy N. Spooner's letter against war-material exports
subfiles.from: Roy N. Spooner
subfiles.about: Urges the President to end American traffic in war materials with Japan.
subfiles.summary: Spooner calls the volume of American war materials supplied to Japan deeply disturbing. He says the traffic makes the United States a partner in the destruction of Chinese lives and property.

subfiles.title: Reply to Roy N. Spooner
subfiles.from: Edgar P. Allen, Acting Chief, Office of Arms and Munitions Control
subfiles.about: Explains the legal and policy reasons for not invoking an arms embargo.
subfiles.summary: Allen states that a presidential war proclamation would immediately prohibit arms exports to both China and Japan. He says the President had decided that invocation would not serve American interests and reports the value of export licenses issued to each country.

subfiles.title: American League for Peace and Democracy letter to President Roosevelt
subfiles.from: Edwin L. Noble, chairman, Dover branch of the American League for Peace and Democracy
subfiles.about: Appeals to the President to deny Japan American war materials, aircraft, and scrap iron.
subfiles.summary: Noble cites newspaper casualty figures for Chinese civilians, including victims of raids on Canton. He claims that large American sales of war material and aircraft enable Japanese attacks and asks Roosevelt to stop such assistance.
keywords: American League for Peace and Democracy

subfiles.title: American League for Peace and Democracy letter to Cordell Hull
subfiles.from: Edwin L. Noble, chairman, Dover branch of the American League for Peace and Democracy
subfiles.about: Sends Hull a parallel appeal to end American material assistance to Japan.
subfiles.summary: The letter repeats allegations that Japanese aircraft killed thousands of Chinese civilians and that raids on Canton caused further mass casualties. It cites American sales of war materials and airplanes and asks Hull to deny the aggressors further support.

subfiles.title: Combined reply to Edwin L. Noble
subfiles.from: Edgar P. Allen, Acting Chief, Office of Arms and Munitions Control
subfiles.about: Acknowledges Noble's two letters and states the administration's legal position on an embargo.
subfiles.summary: Allen says the Neutrality Act would prohibit arms exports to both China and Japan only after a presidential proclamation and that the President considered invocation contrary to national interests. He supplies export-license figures and recalls Hull's June 11 condemnation of bombing civilians and of its material encouragement, especially through bombing-plane manufacture.

subfiles.title: Harold W. Schenck's protest against American aid to Japan
subfiles.from: Harold W. Schenck
subfiles.about: Calls for a prohibition on all war supplies and convertible raw materials exported to Japan.
subfiles.summary: Schenck, recently returned after seven years in Japan, warns that the conflict threatens stability throughout the Pacific and calls American supply of the aggressor hypocritical. Citing Senator Pope and Eliot Janeway, he argues that Japan could not sustain the war without American materials and asks the United States to cease complicity while maintaining friendship with the Japanese people.

subfiles.title: Reply to Harold W. Schenck
subfiles.from: Charles W. Yost, Acting Chief, Office of Arms and Munitions Control
subfiles.about: Explains why neither arms nor broader raw-material exports to Japan had been prohibited.
subfiles.summary: Yost states that a proclamation under the Joint Resolution would embargo arms to both belligerents and that the law gives no power to prohibit other commodities. He defends the President's decision not to invoke it and provides current arms-export licensing figures.

subfiles.title: Mr. and Mrs. J. F. Davis's letter opposing munitions shipments
subfiles.from: Mr. and Mrs. J. F. Davis
subfiles.about: Supports a church petition and urges drastic action against those sending munitions to Japan.
subfiles.summary: The elderly Hollywood correspondents say they learned by radio that Roy L. Smith's church had petitioned against munitions shipments. They express disbelief that American trade supports killings in China and call for a law imposing serious penalties on the sellers.

subfiles.title: Reply to Mr. and Mrs. J. F. Davis
subfiles.from: Charles W. Yost, Acting Chief, Office of Arms and Munitions Control
subfiles.to: Mr. and Mrs. J. F. Davis
subfiles.about: Answers the Davises' protest against exporting war materials to Japan.
subfiles.summary: Yost again explains that the Neutrality Act requires a presidential proclamation and would embargo both belligerents rather than Japan alone. He defends the President's policy, reports export-license values, and cites Hull's public opposition to bombing civilians and supplying bombing planes.

subfiles.title: E. Daryl Mabee's appeal for material action against Japan
subfiles.from: E. Daryl Mabee
subfiles.about: Argues that diplomatic protests are inadequate while American materials continue to support Japan's war and bombing campaigns.
subfiles.summary: Mabee supports official denunciations of bombing civilians but contends that an aggressor will not be restrained by moral shame or diplomatic notes. Citing Canton and Japan's territorial ambitions, he asks the United States to stop exporting all direct and indirect war materials, including scrap iron.

subfiles.title: Reply to E. Daryl Mabee
subfiles.from: Charles W. Yost, Acting Chief, Office of Arms and Munitions Control
subfiles.about: Responds to Mabee's call for restrictions on war materials supplied to Japan.
subfiles.summary: Yost explains that the Neutrality Act could halt arms shipments only after a presidential proclamation and cannot cover commodities beyond the statutory arms list. He gives export-license figures and thanks Mabee for supporting the government's stand against supplying aeronautical equipment to countries bombing civilians.

subfiles.title: Clementine G. Herman's letter on scrap-iron exports
subfiles.from: Clementine G. Herman
subfiles.about: Asks the President to stop American scrap-iron shipments that enable Japan's warfare in China.
subfiles.summary: Herman says American scrap iron enables Japan to continue a merciless slaughter in China. Writing as secretary of a Los Angeles missionary society, she urges Roosevelt to use all his power to halt such shipments.

subfiles.title: Reply to Clementine G. Herman
subfiles.from: Edgar P. Allen, Acting Chief, Office of Arms and Munitions Control
subfiles.about: Explains that existing neutrality legislation does not authorize the President to prohibit scrap-iron exports.
subfiles.summary: Allen says the Neutrality Act permits restrictions on arms, ammunition, and implements of war but expressly excludes raw materials such as scrap iron. He states that no current statute permits the President to stop scrap-iron exports to Japan or any other country and encloses explanatory materials.

subfiles.title: Trinity Reformed Church petition to invoke the Neutrality Act
subfiles.from: Jacob G. Brouwer and members of Trinity Reformed Church
subfiles.about: Asks the President to consider invoking the Neutrality Act to stop American implements of war from reaching Japan.
subfiles.summary: Brouwer says a Reformed Church newspaper editorial persuaded congregants that American supplies were enabling Japanese atrocities against civilians and children. The letter invokes a biblical duty to rescue victims and is followed by several pages of signatures, many poorly legible in the OCR.

subfiles.title: Editorial: China, Japan, America, and War
subfiles.from: The Intelligencer-Leader
subfiles.about: Argues that American exports of scrap iron, oil, steel, aircraft, and credit make the United States complicit in Japan's devastation of China.
subfiles.summary: The editorial cites trade figures, the bombing of Canton, Eliot Janeway's analysis, and Senate debate to claim that Japan could not sustain its campaign without American materials and possible credit. It condemns resolutions against civilian bombing as ineffective while exports continue and urges Christians to write or wire Roosevelt demanding application of the neutrality law.
